results.title: A most fascinating place for anyone interested in culture
results.text: This temple is a place where the families of those who are dying or recently died find a place. Staff assist the family in the cremation process and also provide a hospital of sorts for those dying to come. Across the river from the cremation pyres many people come to sit and watch. It's a fascinating process, meant to be observed with dignity and silence.

results.title: One of the holiest sites in Hinduism
results.text: Pashupatinath is a Shiva Temple and a major pilgrimage site for Hindus.  There is the main temple and many smaller temples on the grounds.  The structures straddle the Bagmati River which is ritually pure and holy but terribly polluted.  There is so much going here it is advisable to read about the site before visiting.  People line up to get inside to worship the linga which is the representation/presence of lord Shiva.  This is open to the Hindu only so unless you are Hindu you cannot enter.  I have met people in India who on the mention of Nepal say that they hope to make a pilgimmage to this Temple before they die.    On the ghats or platforms on the river side of the temple cremations are constantly occurring.  This may be shocking to people from developed countries but it is great example of how close the Nepali people are to the rhythms and cycles of life.  I remember one visit where cremations, children playing in the river and women washing clothes were taking place within 100 feet of one another.  There is a also a building on the upstream side of the river.  It is called a nursing home by locals.  Families bring people about to die here and the people who run the place are good at knowing when death its imminent. Individual are brought to the river's edge and placed on a slanted ramp with their feet in the waters of the river - the belief is that if a person's feet are in the Bagmati's waters at the moment of death s/he will be liberated from the cycles of reincarnation.  There is also an old age home and a small infirmary run by the nuns of Mother Theresa's order.    Cross the bridge and walk up the steps to the smaller temples and you will see numerous sadhus who are devotees of Shiva and make various claims about their diets and abilities to perform various feats. Pashupatinath is a kaleidoscope of activity - a must see.

results.title: Holy visit with family
results.text:
Had a very different experience to visit this temple. Considered one of the biggest and oldest temple for Lord Shiva. Devotees from all over the world can be seen in large numbers every day.

A quick visit is worth. Felt little uncomfortable with the cremation area.

results.title: Very Intersting, get a guide
results.text: There is so much there to see wiht so much significance, pay the extra $10=$20 for a guide, you will learn a lot more than just wandering around.  Don't be surprised by the cremations going on right in front of you with spectator seating.

results.title: an eye-opening encounter
results.text: We have heard about the Hindu rituals but this was our first encounter, an eye-opening experience. The funeral and cremation processes were done according to Nepalese traditions, there were no crying and howling for the deceased, showing that the Nepalese had their own understanding about death. Other sections were off limit to non Hindus.

results.title: Must see if you are in Kathmandu
results.text:
Pashupatinath has not been damaged much by th April 2015 earthquake. It is very interesting to walk around the area alongside the Bagmati River.  the Temple is Napls most important Hindu Temple.
The Sadhus will have their photo taken foor a small amount of money.  Non Hindus cannot enter the main temple.

results.title: Special but interesting experience
results.text:
We walked from Boudda to Pashupatinath in about 30 minutes. We went there from the hill side passing the river and some small buildings looking like an older temple, where a lot of monkeys lived.
We passed a guard, where we paid 1000 rs each and got a ticked. The path from the hill side can be a bit steep at som places.
When we arrived to the crematorium a funeral ritual just started. It was really interresting to see the hindu culture, but also a bit stange to be watching as a tourist. It's different from our culture, to burn dead family members outside while watching, so some people might find it a bit macabre.
But it was a very peacefull and quiet cermony, which gave us a good insight in the hindu culture.

If you want to take pictures of the painted men sitting outside the temple, they will charge you.

results.title: Fascinating place
results.text:
It is a magical place where one can sit and think about life and death at the very same moment.
Best moment to visit in our opinion is just before sunset.
Having been more than once to Varanasi (the Indian holy city on the banks of Ganges), we can definitely say thay Pashupatinath has kept its authenticity better with time passing... You will not be bothered by touts: the only "tourist attraction" there seems to be "businness-sadhus" and it's up to you to give them a few Rupies and have a funny photo together if you want.

results.title: Sacred Hindu temple
results.text: We visited this during our Nepal trip in December 2010. The Pashupatinath Temple is a very popular sacred Hindu temple dedicated to Lord Shiva(Pashupatinath) and is located on the banks of the Bagmati River 5 kilometres north-east of Kathmandu Valley.This is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Photography is not allowed inside the temple complex, which is very well maintained. We helped by a priest did small puja inside the temple premises and the priest was happy with whatever we payed at the end unlike some temples in India. Only Hindus are allowed to enter the temple premises. Must visit when in Kathmandu.
